text:
1. PRIMARY DIAGNOSIS
- Root cause: The CNC router controller is very likely entering a self-protective thermal shutdown or lock-up due to inadequate cooling, triggered by a failing cabinet fan running at reduced airflow and generating noise bearing failure. The intermittent nature — stalling mid-job with no logged alarm — points to a non-latching hardware monitor, such as an embedded temperature sensor on the main controller board, that cuts drive signals silently. Resuming after reboot aligns with thermal recovery; the fan noise confirms the cooling path is compromised.
- This diagnosis is built on the pattern of “stall, no alarm, silence, reboot restores” commonly seen in dedicated CNC motion controllers (e.g., Centroid, LinuxCNC with Mesa cards, or proprietary PC-based systems) when the CPU or motion FPGA exceeds its thermal envelope. High ambient humidity exacerbates airflow restrictions by promoting dust adhesion on heatsinks and can enable subtle leakage currents on exposed board traces, increasing controller instability.
- No specific error codes are provided, but the absence of a visible alarm is itself a diagnostic clue: it rules out most axis limit, servo drive fault, or emergency-stop events that would write to a log. Instead, the fault lands in the category of unlogged system crashes, strongly implicating power or thermal margins.
- Confidence: 65%. The data is insufficient to pinpoint the exact component without measurements, but this is the highest-probability first-line hypothesis given the reported symptoms. A list of “Data Needed” follows.
  - Data Needed: The exact make and model of the CNC controller, motion drives, and fan unit, along with any available firmware version.
  - Data Needed: Cabinet internal ambient temperature measured at the controller board with a calibrated probe, both at idle and after 20 minutes of a typical cutting program (when stall is most likely). Acceptable range is typically 0–50°C but many systems derate above 35°C.
  - Data Needed: The fan’s actual RPM or airflow reading versus its specification (often 80–120 CFM for a 120mm cabinet fan). Noise alone confirms bearing wear; a failing bearing often drops RPM by 30% or more.
  - Data Needed: Voltage readings of the controller’s logic power supply (often 5V or 24V DC) captured with an oscilloscope at the moment of stall, looking for sags, spikes, or ripple exceeding ±5%.
  - Data Needed: A physical inspection of all circuit boards for dust, coolant mist residue, or signs of corrosion — especially on connectors and exposed vias, given the high-humidity environment.
  - Data Needed: A complete extraction of any hidden error logs or diagnostic screens from the controller software (e.g., LinuxCNC’s HAL status, Mach4’s diagnostic panel, or the OEM’s maintenance interface). Even “no alarm” sometimes still records a software watchdog timeout.

2. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS
- Alternative cause 1: Intermittent power supply droop under load (high likelihood). Switching power supplies in industrial cabinets can degrade with heat and age; their output capacitors dry out, causing a momentary voltage drop that crashes the controller without a latching alarm. Ruled in by power-supply testing and ruled out if the DC bus remains stable during stall.
- Alternative cause 2: Electrical noise coupling into logic signals (medium likelihood). A noisy fan motor can radiate electromagnetic interference (EMI) that corrupts step/direction pulses or encoder feedback. Combined with high humidity, corrosion on shielding connections reduces immunity. Ruled in by placing a portable AM radio near the cabinet to listen for static bursts correlated with the fan.
- Alternative cause 3: Moisture-induced corrosion or condensation on the controller board (medium likelihood). High humidity, especially if the machine is in an unheated space subject to temperature swings, can lead to invisible short circuits on increasingly dense surface-mount pads. This can cause random latencies or crashes without permanent damage. Ruled in by board inspection under magnification; ruled out if the board is conformally coated and dry.
- Alternative cause 4: Ground loop or poor earth grounding causing reference shift (lower likelihood). A noisy fan can inject current into the ground plane; if the controller’s logic ground is not properly bonded, this can raise the ground potential and glitch digital signals. This is classic in custom CNC machines where wiring is added without star-ground discipline. Ruled in by measuring AC voltage between cabinet chassis and machine frame during operation.

3. DIAGNOSTIC VERIFICATION
- Test: Measure the internal cabinet temperature at the CPU/chipset heatsink using a thermocouple or IR thermometer through a small port (avoid opening the door during test, as that changes airflow). Record the trend from a cold start until the stall occurs. A reading above 70°C on the chip case strongly correlates with thermal shutdown. This takes 30 minutes and a $30 temperature logger.
- Test: Perform an airflow bench test of the noisy fan: remove it, clean it, and measure RPM with a photo tachometer while applying its rated voltage (typically 12 or 24V DC) on the bench. Compare to the specification printed on the fan label. A drop of more than 20% from the rated RPM demands immediate replacement. A new fan costs $15–$50; the test takes 0.3 hours.
- Test: Monitor the controller’s logic voltage with a digital storage oscilloscope set to single-sequence capture, triggering on a 5% drop from nominal. Place the probe directly at the controller’s power input terminals. Run a stress program (air-cutting a complex 3D path) to replicate the stall. If captured, the drop confirms power supply failure. Oscilloscope rental costs about $40/day; a technician’s diagnostic hour is ~$100–150.
- Test: Use the controller’s built-in diagnostic utilities to log drive command lag or real-time jitter. In LinuxCNC, the “latency-test” utility run for 10 minutes will expose excessive jitter that can cause a stall; in Mach, the QA test shows interrupts. Jitter above 15–20 µs on a 1 kHz servo thread is a cause for failure. This test is zero cost and should be done first.

4. SHOP INTERROGATION
- “Can you show me the temperature log inside the controller cabinet during a full program run? Were any temperatures recorded above the manufacturer’s maximum operating rating for the motion controller?”
- "What is the measured RPM of that noisy fan, and how does it compare to the rating on the fan label? Did you check airflow with an anemometer?"
- "When the machine stalls, have you probed the DC logic supply with an oscilloscope to rule out a power sag? If not, why are we skipping the most basic check?"
- "Have you pulled the controller board and inspected it under a microscope for moisture or corrosion, given the operator’s note about high humidity? What did you find?"
- "If you believe this is a software crash, can you show me the kernel log or the controller’s error log from the exact time of the stall, showing what process halted? No log means no diagnostic basis for a software claim."

5. CONVERSATION SCRIPTING
- Opening: "I’ve been reading up on intermittent CNC stalls when cooling is marginal, and I want to make sure we’re methodical. Could you walk me through the tests you’ve already done on the cabinet cooling and power supply?"
- Phrasing: Frame every request as a desire to understand, not to challenge. "I’m curious—did the fan RPM measure at spec when you checked it? I’ve seen bearings seize and still spin, but below needed speed."
- Example dialogue for power question: "I learned that a lot of motion controllers crash silently if the 5V rail dips for even a few milliseconds. Did you have a chance to scope that rail while the machine was running a program? I’d love to see that waveform if you captured it."
- Body language: Stand at ease, keep a notepad, glance at the machine while talking, nod at technical details—signal you're a fellow troubleshooter, not a plaintiff.
- Response handling (if defensive): "I’m not doubting your experience. I just need to authorize repairs that follow a logical test path, because replacing parts on a hunch can get expensive fast in these custom machines. Let’s work together to isolate it."
- Exit strategy: "I appreciate the time. Let me review these findings and the quote you’ll email. I’ll give you a go-ahead once I confirm the test plan lines up with the controller’s service manual."
- NEVER say: "My AI report says..." or "I got a second opinion online." ALWAYS say: "I’ve done some reading on these types of intermittent faults and want to make sure we check the basics first."

6. COST BREAKDOWN
- Parts: A quality replacement cooling fan (e.g., a 120mm ball-bearing 24V unit from a brand like Sunon or Delta) costs $18–45 from standard industrial suppliers, not more than $60 even with rush shipping. If the controller power supply needs replacement, a Mean Well 5V/12V enclosed supply runs $30–80.
- Labor: A competent CNC technician should diagnose this in 1.5–2.0 hours, covering temperature logging, voltage monitoring, fan bench test, and log review. At a typical industrial service rate of $125–150 per hour, diagnostic labor totals $190–300.
- Total fair price range: If the fan alone fixes it, $210–360 (1.5 hr diagnostic + $45 fan). If a power supply joins, $290–450. Any quote exceeding $600 for “electronic diagnostics and fan” without showing captured waveform data is suspect.
- Overcharge identifiers: A quote for a “full controller board replacement” without documentation of overheating or power failure. A “software reload/reinstall” as the first step without hardware checks. Stacked service fees for “electrical inspection” and “troubleshooting” that aren’t itemized.

7. RIPOFF DETECTION
- Parts cannon: The shop wants to immediately replace the entire motion controller or the PC, arguing “these things just fail,” when the only evidence is a noisy fan. That skips the basic thermal and power checks.
- Diagnostic shortcuts: The tech arrives, hears the fan, says “fan is bad, but the controller probably needs an upgrade too,” and offers a lump sum without recording a single measurement.
- Price gouging: Charging $200 or more for a generic cabinet fan, or 4+ hours for a “CNC system analysis” that consists of listening to the fan and rebooting the machine. Labor rates above $175/hr in an area dominated by machine shops may be normal, but the hours must be justified with a test log.

8. AUTHORIZATION GUIDE
- Approve immediately: One hour of labor for the diagnostic verification tests outlined — temperature logging, voltage capture attempt, fan bench test, and log extraction. If the fan fails the RPM test, approve its replacement (part + 0.5 hr labor) because a failing fan is a certainty regardless of the stall’s root cause.
- Reject outright: Any proposal to swap the controller mainboard, PC, or motion drives without first documenting thermal or power anomalies. A “full cabinet re-wire” or “grounding upgrade” as a first step, when the measured ground noise is unknown.
- Get a second opinion: If the shop refuses to show any logged data or claims their diagnostic software “covers everything” but gives you a verbal-only verdict, retrieve the machine’s SD card or hard drive log and consult a controls engineer who specializes in the specific controller platform (e.g., Centroid community or LinuxCNC forum experts).

9. TECHNICAL EDUCATION
- System operation: A CNC controller is a dedicated industrial computer that processes G-code into precisely timed step/direction pulses (or analog velocity commands) to servo/stepper drives. It relies on a regulated DC power supply and stable thermal environment. Most controllers embed a temperature sensor in the CPU or FPGA that will throttle or halt operations if the internal die temperature exceeds safe limits (often 85–100°C). This shutdown is often invisible to the user—no alarm, just stopped motion.
- Failure mechanism: A noisy fan indicates worn bearings, which reduce blade speed. Reduced airflow allows the cabinet’s internal temperature to climb, especially during long jobs when the drives and controller heat up. At a critical temperature, the controller’s internal watchdog may mute all outputs to prevent damage, but it doesn’t always latch an error because the power isn’t cycled—it’s a logic freeze. Simultaneously, high humidity causes dust to clump on heatsinks, insulating them further, and can cause slight electrical leakage on unprotected PCBs, lowering the noise margin for digital signals.
- Prevention: After repairing, install a filtered fan with a tachometer output that can be monitored by the controller’s I/O. Set a software alarm if fan RPM drops below a threshold. Add a cabinet temperature sensor ($20 thermistor) wired to an input so the controller can pause the program before shutdown. Operate the machine in a humidity-controlled space, or add a small cabinet heater to keep internal components above dew point during off hours.

10. OEM PARTS STRATEGY
- Fan: If the machine builder used a specific brand (e.g., Rittal, Hoffman panel fan), obtain the exact replacement part number from their BOM to ensure the correct airflow curve and connector. For a generic retrofit, a Sunon SF121X series (24V, 120mm, 100 CFM) with ball bearings is a robust choice. For example, Sunon PF92251V1-000U-A99 (92mm) might be used. Check the old fan’s label before buying.
- Controller power supply: If a standard enclosed supply, use the exact model from the manufacturer (Mean Well, Cosel, etc.) to preserve mounting holes and voltage adjustment range. A Mean Well RS-150-5 (5V 26A) is common for logic. Always buy from authorized distributors to avoid counterfeit units with insufficient capacitors.
- Why OEM/cross: Using a fan with lower airflow (common cheap replacements) will bring back the thermal problem. Using a supply with higher ripple can introduce new noise issues. Stick to the voltages and current ratings on the original labels.
- Pricing sources: Digi-Key, Mouser, AutomationDirect for fans and supplies; for controller-specific parts (if needed), the manufacturer’s parts store (Centroid, Mesa, etc.).

11. NEGOTIATION TACTICS
- Ask for a detailed breakdown of the diagnostic time and test equipment used. If they claim “3 hours of electronic troubleshooting,” request the scope captures and temperature logs. Without them, negotiate down to the 1.5 hours a basic verification requires.
- Quote the cost of the fan yourself: “I can supply the same Sunon fan for $35 from Mouser; can you match that plus 0.3 hours to install?” Many shops will agree to avoid losing the labor. For power supplies, “Mean Well equivalent is $55; I’m not paying $200 for a no-name.”
- If the shop insists on replacing the controller, walk away immediately and seek a second opinion from an independent CNC retrofitter. The value of these custom machines lies in the controller and drives; replacing the brain without a confirmed failure is a $2,000–5,000 gamble. The walk-away point is a quote over $600 with no captured data, or any pressure to authorize a full control upgrade.

12. LIKELY CAUSES (RANKED)
- Primary cause: Thermal shutdown of the motion controller due to a failed cooling fan and elevated cabinet temperature — 65% confidence. The noisy fan, high-humidity environment, and no-error stall with reboot recovery are textbook for this.
- Secondary cause: Intermittent power supply voltage collapse under load — 20% confidence. This fits the silent stall pattern, but would usually also corrupt the reboot process or leave a power-OK fault in the log if monitored.
- Tertiary cause: Noise-induced signaling faults from the failing fan motor or corroded grounds — 15% confidence. The fan noise provides a physical source of EMI; high humidity reduces shielding effectiveness. This would cause random stalls independent of job length, potentially earlier.

13. RECOMMENDATIONS
- Immediate action: Before running another job, open the cabinet (power off) and carefully vacuum/clean all heatsinks, filters, and the fan intake. Check for pluggage. Then, replace the noisy fan with a known-good unit of the same specification. This eliminates the most obvious and cheapest variable, even if it doesn’t solve the stall.
- Future maintenance schedule: Every 3 months, blow out the control cabinet with dry, filtered compressed air and inspect the fan for noise. Every 6 months, verify the cabinet temperature during a long run and log it. Once a year, check all screw terminals for torque and look for any corrosion, especially in high-humidity shops.
- Warning signs to monitor: If the fan noise returns within weeks, suspect bearing contamination — install a filtered fan. If the machine stalls after shorter and shorter run times, the underlying thermal problem is worsening aggressively. If the controller begins to corrupt tool offsets or lose position before stalling, it may indicate a failing power supply capacitor bank, not just thermal.

14. SOURCE VERIFICATION
- CNCzone.com: Search “CNC router stalls mid job no error” — multiple threads detail identical symptoms caused by overheating PC-based controllers and solve them with cabinet cooling upgrades. These are real-world technician experiences, not vendor ads.
- LinuxCNC documentation (linuxcnc.org/docs/): The “Latency Test” and “Troubleshooting” sections explain how excessive jitter or thermal throttling can halt motion without a pop-up error. Applies to many open-source controllers used in custom routers.
- Centroid CNC Tech Bulletins: Bulletins 256 and 312 describe proper cabinet cooling and grounding practices for their Acorn/Oak boards, warning of thermal shutdown without alarm if the CPU temperature exceeds limits. Available via centroidcnc.com/support.
- Practical Machinist forums: The “CNC Machine Troubleshooting” area contains multiple case studies where “controller crashes and resets” were traced to power supply dying under load or a fan seizing, documented with scope captures.

15. NEXT STEPS SUMMARY
- First, measure the cabinet temperature during a simulated job and replace the noisy fan immediately if RPM is below spec (or simply preemptively replace it — it’s failing). This addresses the most probable cause at minimal cost.
- Second, if stalls persist, attach an oscilloscope to the controller’s DC supply and capture a trigger event during the stall to test for power droop; meanwhile extract any hidden error logs.
- Third, after correcting the thermal/power issue, install a cabinet temperature sensor and fan RPM monitor tied to the controller’s I/O to prevent future unlogged shutdowns.
